cards.title: What Is a Domain Service?
cards.teaser: A domain service is a stateless operation that belongs in the domain layer but cannot naturally live on any single entity or value object — it expresses a domain concept, enforces invariants, and speaks the ubiquitous language.

runs.text: Eric Evans introduced the term in
Domain-Driven Design
(2003): "When a significant process or transformation in the domain is not a natural responsibility of an
entity
or
value object
, add an operation to the model as a standalone interface declared as a
service
." The key phrase is "not a natural responsibility" — a domain service is not an escape hatch for laziness; it is the right home for operations the domain genuinely cannot assign to one object.
Three criteria from Evans identify a good domain service candidate:

items.text: — it expresses a concept that domain experts name and discuss.
— all information needed to perform the operation is passed as arguments; nothing is stored on the service instance between calls.
It does not fit on an entity or value object
— placing it there would make the entity bloated or give it an awkward responsibility.

runs.text: A domain service is
not
a utility class, a repository, an application coordinator, or an infrastructure adapter. It is domain logic — pure, expressive, and testable.

The word "service" in DDD is overloaded. Evans specifically distinguishes domain services (pure domain logic) from application services (use-case coordination) and infrastructure services (technical concerns). All three exist; confusing them is the root of most service-layer mistakes.

A domain service is a named domain operation that doesn't naturally live on any single entity or value object. It is stateless, speaks the domain language, and enforces domain rules — not application flow or technical concerns.

cards.title: When to Reach for a Domain Service
cards.teaser: Two signals indicate you need a domain service: the operation genuinely spans multiple aggregates, or the operation expresses a domain concept that domain experts name but that doesn't belong to any single entity.

runs.text: The most common case is an operation that must read or mutate
two or more aggregates
. Because aggregates are the consistency boundary, no single aggregate can own an operation that crosses boundaries. A
MoneyTransferService
that debits one
Account
and credits another is the canonical example: neither account owns the transfer concept.

The second case is a domain concept that domain experts name explicitly — "calculate shipping," "price the order," "validate eligibility" — but that doesn't belong on any single entity without creating an awkward responsibility:

items.text: — TransferMoney(from: Account, to: Account, amount: Money)
Named domain concept with multi-party involvement
— ShippingCalculator(order: Order, warehouse: Warehouse, carrier: Carrier)
— CreditLimitChecker(customer: Customer, order: Order, ledger: CreditLedger)
— CurrencyConverter(amount: Money, targetCurrency: Currency, rates: ExchangeRates)

runs.text: Notice that in every case the service name comes from the ubiquitous language. Domain experts say "transfer money," "calculate shipping," "check credit limit" — these are domain service names, not implementation artifacts.

Ask before extracting: "Would domain experts use this verb in conversation?" If they would say 'calculate shipping' but not 'process entity logic', the first is a domain service name and the second is a symptom of anemic thinking.

Reach for a domain service when an operation genuinely involves multiple aggregates, or when domain experts name an operation that doesn't fit cleanly inside one entity. If neither condition is true, put the logic on the entity.

cards.title: Domain Service vs Application Service
cards.teaser: A domain service enforces domain invariants; an application service orchestrates a use case. The domain service has no idea what HTTP, queues, or databases are. The application service knows all about them and calls the domain service to do the real work.

runs.text: This is the most important distinction in layered DDD architecture, and the one most frequently collapsed. The difference can be stated precisely:

items.text: — implements domain logic that enforces invariants or computes domain-significant results. It takes domain objects as arguments and returns domain objects. It has no knowledge of persistence, HTTP, messaging, or transaction management.

— implements a use case ("transfer funds," "place order"). It loads aggregates from repositories, calls domain services and aggregate methods to do the real work, then persists changes. It owns the transaction boundary and handles cross-cutting concerns (authorization, logging, event publishing).

runs.text: A concrete contrast:
The domain service knows nothing about
AccountRepository
, transactions, or events. The application service knows nothing about debit/credit invariants. Each layer owns its own concerns.

Domain services do the domain thinking; application services do the coordination. The domain service enforces the rule that you can't debit more than your balance. The application service loads the account, calls the domain service, and saves the result.

cards.title: Domain Service vs Infrastructure Service
cards.teaser: A domain service is pure — it works on domain objects and has no technical dependencies. An infrastructure service has technical concerns: sending email, persisting to a database, calling a payment gateway. The line is technology.

runs.text: Both domain services and infrastructure services are sometimes called "services," which creates confusion. The clean separator is: does it depend on any technology outside the domain model?

items.text: — inputs and outputs are domain objects. No I/O. No network calls. No database queries. Could run in a test with zero mocking infrastructure. Example:
that applies discount rules to a
(database read model). They live in the infrastructure layer, behind an interface defined in the domain or application layer.

runs.text: A subtle but important case: what if a domain service needs data from an external system (e.g., current exchange rates)? The domain service declares an
interface
for what it needs (e.g.,
ExchangeRateProvider

) and accepts it as a dependency. The implementation of that interface lives in the infrastructure layer. This is the Dependency Inversion Principle applied to domain services: the domain defines the abstraction; infrastructure fulfills it.

Ask the purity question: "Can I test this service in a unit test with no mocks?" If yes, it is likely a domain service. If it requires mocking a database, HTTP client, or file system, it is an infrastructure service — or a domain service that has been contaminated with infrastructure concerns.

Domain services touch only domain objects. Infrastructure services touch technology — databases, email, payment APIs. If a service sends an email, it's infrastructure. If it calculates a discount, it's domain.

cards.title: Statelessness — The Core Constraint
cards.teaser: A domain service holds no instance state between calls. Every call gets everything it needs through its parameters. This constraint is what makes domain services safe to share as singletons and trivial to reason about.

runs.text: Statelessness is not incidental — it is definitional. Evans explicitly states that a domain service is "stateless" and that this is what distinguishes it from an entity. An entity has identity and state that evolves over time. A domain service has neither.
Concretely, statelessness means:

items.text: — the service struct or class has no
fields that accumulate state between calls.
twice with the same arguments produces the same result each time (assuming the input aggregates haven't changed).
— because there is no mutable shared state, a stateless domain service can be called concurrently without synchronization.
— one instance of the service can serve the entire application. The DI container can create it once.

runs.text: Configuration injected at construction (like
ExchangeRateProvider
or a
FeePolicy
value object) does not violate statelessness — those are
dependencies
, not accumulated operation state. The service does not change them between calls.

A domain service carries no memory between calls. Give it the same inputs twice and you get the same answer twice. That's what stateless means — and it's why you can safely share one instance across the whole app.

cards.title: Naming Domain Services
cards.teaser: Domain service names are verb phrases drawn from the ubiquitous language — MoneyTransferService, ShippingCalculator, CreditLimitChecker. The name should make domain experts nod, not squint.

runs.text: Because domain services express domain concepts, their names must come from the ubiquitous language — the shared vocabulary agreed on with domain experts. A service name that sounds like an implementation artifact (
DataProcessor
BusinessLogicHandler
EntityManager
) is a warning sign: either the service should not exist, or the naming has drifted from the domain.
Conventions that work well:

items.text: . The verb-noun form emphasizes the operation.
. The domain noun anchors the concept; the suffix indicates role.
show the name to a domain expert. If they immediately understand what it does, the name is right. If they ask "what does that mean?", rename it.

runs.text: Names to avoid:

items.text: (too broad; a bag for anything account-related)
(these are repository/application-layer responsibilities, not domain services)

runs.text: Name your domain service so a domain expert can read it and immediately know what it does. If the name sounds like a database term or a tech buzzword, it belongs somewhere else — or needs a better name.

cards.title: The Over-Use Anti-Pattern: The Anemic Domain Model
cards.teaser: The deadliest misuse of domain services is extracting all logic out of entities into services, leaving entities as dumb data bags. Martin Fowler named this the Anemic Domain Model — it looks like OOP but is actually procedural code in disguise.

runs.text: Martin Fowler described the
Anemic Domain Model

anti-pattern in 2003: domain objects that contain only fields and getters/setters, with all business logic pushed into service objects. The result is a domain model with no behavior — just a thin data layer with a separate procedural logic layer.

The anemic trap is seductive because it feels organized: "all logic goes in services, all data goes in models." But it violates encapsulation and removes the most powerful benefit of OOP — the ability to model behavior alongside the data it operates on.

If you find yourself writing a domain service that reads one entity's fields, applies logic, and writes results back to the same entity, you have an anemic model. That logic belongs on the entity. Domain services are for operations that genuinely span multiple aggregates or express concepts that don't belong to any single one.

The anemic domain model puts all logic in services and leaves entities as empty data holders. It looks neat but it's actually just procedural code — the domain model has no real behavior, so it can't enforce its own invariants.

cards.title: When NOT to Extract a Domain Service
cards.teaser: If the operation clearly belongs to one entity — it uses only that entity's data, enforces that entity's invariants, and makes sense as that entity's method — leave it on the entity. Premature extraction is as harmful as under-extraction.

runs.text: The heuristic is straightforward: if the operation answers a question about one aggregate, or changes the state of one aggregate according to that aggregate's own rules, it belongs on the aggregate. Extract a service only when the operation cannot be naturally placed on any single aggregate.

Evans warns: "Be cautious about creating domain services. Any time you think you need a service, first check whether the operation can naturally fit on an entity or value object. Services should be the exception, not the rule."

Before creating a domain service, ask: 'Does this operation use only one entity's data and enforce only that entity's rules?' If yes, it's a method on the entity. Services are for the exceptions — operations that genuinely span multiple aggregates.

cards.title: The TransferMoney Domain Service — A Full Example
cards.teaser: TransferMoney is the textbook domain service: it coordinates two Account aggregates, enforces cross-aggregate invariants, and expresses a concept domain experts name explicitly. It belongs neither on the source nor the destination account.

runs.text: The money transfer example illustrates every property of a well-designed domain service:

items.text: — domain experts say "transfer money"; the service is
aggregates; neither can own the operation.
— no instance state; takes inputs, returns outputs.
— no database, no network, no side effects beyond modifying the passed-in domain objects.
(entity enforces its own overdraft rule) and

runs.text: The service is only 5 lines of logic. All the real invariant checking happens inside the entities. The service's job is coordination across the aggregate boundary — nothing more.

TransferMoney is the simplest possible domain service: it calls debit on one account and credit on the other. The actual rules — can't overdraw, must be active — live on each account, where they belong.

cards.title: Domain Service Composition
cards.teaser: Domain services can call other domain services. A higher-level operation that coordinates two sub-operations — each of which is its own domain service — is itself a domain service, provided it remains pure and stateless.

runs.text: Composition of domain services is natural and encouraged when it reflects the domain model. If the domain experts describe a process in terms of sub-processes that are each domain-significant, the composition should appear explicitly in code.
Example: an
OrderFulfillmentService
coordinates a
InventoryReservationService
and a
ShippingCalculator
Rules for composed domain services:

items.text: The composing service must remain pure
— it may only call other domain services (or aggregate methods). If it loads repositories or publishes events, it has become an application service.
The composition must express a domain concept
— "fulfill order" is something domain experts discuss. A service that combines two sub-operations purely for technical reuse is not a domain service.
— deep service call hierarchies obscure domain logic. If you need more than two levels of service composition, revisit whether the model is right.

runs.text: Domain services can call each other as long as the composed service remains pure and expresses a real domain concept. The moment a 'domain service' loads a database or publishes an event, it has crossed into application service territory.

cards.title: Domain Services and the Three-Layer Architecture
cards.teaser: Domain services live in the domain layer. Application services live in the application layer above. Infrastructure services live in the infrastructure layer below. Each layer has a strict direction: application calls domain; domain never calls application or infrastructure.

runs.text: DDD's layered architecture has three layers relevant to services:

items.text: — entities, value objects, aggregates, domain services, domain events, repository
. No dependencies on layers above or below.

— application services (use-case coordinators). Depends on the domain layer (calls domain services, aggregate methods). Depends on infrastructure layer abstractions (repository implementations, event publishers) via interfaces defined in the domain layer.
— repository implementations, messaging adapters, external API clients, email senders. Implements interfaces defined in the domain layer.

runs.text: Dependency direction is strictly downward and inward (following the Dependency Rule from Clean Architecture): infrastructure implements domain interfaces; application calls domain logic; domain knows nothing about the layers above it.
Where domain services sit in a typical call chain:

items.text: HTTP controller / queue consumer (infrastructure) calls application service.
Application service loads aggregates from repository.
Application service calls domain service with loaded aggregates.
Domain service calls aggregate methods; returns modified domain objects.
Application service persists changes; publishes domain events.

runs.text: The domain layer is the innermost ring. It must never import from application or infrastructure layers. If your domain service has a repository import or an HTTP client import, the architecture has inverted — fix it by extracting an interface and inverting the dependency.

Think of three rings: domain in the center, application around it, infrastructure on the outside. Domain services live in the center and know nothing about the outer rings. Application services use domain services. Infrastructure implements interfaces the domain defines.

cards.title: Testing Domain Services
cards.teaser: Domain services are the easiest code in the system to test: they take domain objects in and return domain objects out, with no I/O, no mocks, and no framework setup required. A test is literally: construct inputs, call the service, assert the outputs.

runs.text: The testability of domain services is a direct consequence of their purity. Every property that makes them good domain objects — stateless, no side effects, pure inputs and outputs — also makes them trivial to test.

No mocks. No stubs. No database setup. No network. Just domain objects constructed in the test, passed to the service, and assertions on the results. This is the concrete advantage of keeping domain services pure — the feedback loop for testing is instantaneous.

If you need to mock anything to test a domain service, the service is not pure. Infrastructure concerns have leaked in. Extract them behind an interface and inject the mock through the constructor — then the tests become clean again.

Testing a domain service is as simple as it gets: make some domain objects, call the service, check the results. No mocks, no databases, no setup. That's the reward you get for keeping domain logic pure.

cards.title: ShippingCalculator — A Second Pure Domain Service Example
cards.teaser: ShippingCalculator shows that domain services are not just for cross-aggregate mutation — they are equally suited for cross-aggregate computation: deriving a domain-significant value from multiple aggregates without changing any of them.

runs.text: Not all domain services mutate state. Some compute a domain-significant result from multiple inputs without changing anything.
ShippingCalculator
is a classic example: it takes an
Order
, a
Warehouse
, and carrier policy, and returns a
Money
value object — the calculated shipping cost.
Why does this belong in a domain service rather than on
Order
? Because the calculation requires knowledge from
Warehouse
(location, available carriers) and carrier policy that is not owned by any single aggregate. An
Order
that knows about warehouses and carrier policies would violate its own bounded context.
This service is:

— returns a value object, mutates nothing.

runs.text: Domain services are not only for mutations. A service that calculates shipping from order and warehouse data is just as valid — it computes a domain result using multiple aggregates' data without belonging naturally to any one of them.

cards.title: Domain Services as Interfaces
cards.teaser: Define a domain service as a protocol or interface, not a concrete struct. This lets the application layer depend on the abstraction, and lets tests swap in fakes without mocking infrastructure — keeping the domain model flexible and independently deployable.

runs.text: Although domain services should be pure, there are cases where the right approach is to define the service as an
interface
in the domain layer with one or more concrete implementations. This is especially true when:

items.text: The service needs a pluggable algorithm
The service has a pure domain contract but an infrastructure-backed implementation
is a domain interface; the implementation calls an API. The domain service that
it stays pure by accepting the interface as a constructor argument.
that returns a fixed rate keeps tests fast and deterministic.

runs.text: The pattern keeps the domain layer clean:
OrderPricingService
never imports a network library. The infrastructure dependency is injected through the interface at construction time by the application layer's DI container.

Define domain services as protocols when the algorithm can vary or when an implementation touches infrastructure. The domain code depends on the protocol; infrastructure provides the concrete implementation; tests swap in a fake. The domain stays clean.
